meta.scene_summary: We are building a digital future that works perfectly until the bill arrives or the headers get injected.

cooking.headline: X is doing its monthly 'clean the room' routine before the election
cooking.summary: X just purged 13,000 accounts for election meddling, which is a great way to pretend the platform isn't just a giant digital mosh pit. It's the social media equivalent of deleting your browser history right before your parents walk into the room.
cooking.plain_english: The social media platform X removed 13,000 accounts it identified as being involved in efforts to influence upcoming elections.

cooking.headline: Malicious bots are the ultimate remote workers
cooking.summary: When Yandex went offline, the automated bot traffic didn't just disappear; it simply migrated to other targets like a group of coworkers moving to a new Slack channel. It's comforting to know that even in the digital underworld, nobody is actually quitting—they're just finding a more productive place to be annoying.
cooking.plain_english: Data shows that when the search engine Yandex experienced a service outage, the automated malicious traffic targeting it immediately shifted to other online platforms.

cooking.headline: Ubuntu 26.10 is here to remind you that your distro is outdated
cooking.summary: Canonical just released the 'Stonking Stingray,' proving that even Linux distros are subject to the relentless pressure of biannual naming conventions. It's the perfect time to spend your entire weekend fixing dependencies you didn't even know were broken.
cooking.plain_english: The latest version of the Ubuntu operating system, version 26.10, has been officially released to the public.

cooked.headline: Bank of America is paying a thousand people to fix what one AI broke
cooked.summary: Bank of America had to hire a small army of contractors to clean up the mess left behind by the Mythos AI. It turns out that automating your tech stack is a great way to generate full-time employment for everyone who has to patch the fallout.
cooked.plain_english: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to fix security and software issues caused by an artificial intelligence tool called Mythos.

cooked.headline: Banks are trying to return the AI data center debt they just bought
cooked.summary: Banks spent months underwriting massive data center loans, but now they are desperately trying to offload that debt to anyone else. It is the financial equivalent of buying a round of drinks for the whole bar and then asking everyone to venmo you back before the tab arrives.
cooked.plain_english: Financial institutions that provided loans for building AI data centers are now attempting to sell those debts to other investors.

cooked.headline: The AI gold rush is hitting a wall of interest rates
cooked.summary: Building massive data centers to house AI models is expensive, and it turns out that borrowing money to do so isn't free anymore. It's like trying to build an extension on your house while your mortgage lender decides to stop pretending the economy is fine.
cooked.plain_english: High interest rates are making it more expensive for companies to fund the construction of large data centers required for artificial intelligence.

cooked.headline: Ad networks are now the most efficient way to get hacked
cooked.summary: We spent decades perfecting ad-blockers to stop annoying pop-ups, but now they are a prerequisite for not getting your phone turned into a remote surveillance device. It's the ultimate 'I didn't click anything' excuse, except this time it's actually true.
cooked.plain_english: Researchers discovered that digital advertising networks are being used to install spyware on mobile devices without any user interaction.

cooked.headline: Zero-click spyware is the ultimate 'read receipt' nightmare
cooked.summary: The industry has finally achieved the developer dream of 100% engagement rates by removing the need for the user to actually do anything. It turns out that 'zero-click' is great for conversion metrics but absolutely terrible for your personal safety.
cooked.plain_english: A security firm found that malicious software is being delivered via targeted advertisements that infect devices without requiring the user to click on anything.

cooked.headline: Your HTTP headers are now a prompt injection playground
cooked.summary: Researchers found that over 200 million web responses are vulnerable to prompt injection via HTTP headers. It turns out that trusting data from the web is like eating gas station sushi—you really shouldn't, but we keep doing it anyway.
cooked.plain_english: Security experts discovered that many websites contain hidden commands in their server response data that can trick AI systems into performing unauthorized actions.

cooked.headline: Global logistics is having a really bad day at the office
cooked.summary: Geopolitical tensions in the Strait of Hormuz have escalated to the point where actual container ships are being deleted from the production environment. It turns out that 'physical layer' issues are significantly harder to resolve than a standard DNS outage.
cooked.plain_english: A container ship was sunk in the Strait of Hormuz during an attack, disrupting maritime shipping in the region.
